blocks.body: Addition and subtraction are the first two operations of arithmetic. Addition puts two amounts together. Subtraction goes the other way: given a whole and one of its parts, it finds the other part, and that single number answers several different-looking questions, such as how much is left, how much more is needed, and how far apart two numbers are. Splitting numbers into parts ([[composing-decomposing-numbers]]) and tens and ones ([[place-value]]) are assumed.

blocks.title: The two operations
blocks.body: Throughout, numbers are the whole numbers $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$, each of which counts some finite collection of objects. Two collections are disjoint if no object belongs to both. Two laws of addition are used freely below: the commutative law $a + b = b + a$ and the associative law $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$. They are proved on [[properties-of-operations]] and taken on trust here.

blocks.title: Sum
blocks.body:
If a collection $A$ of $a$ objects is put together with a disjoint collection $B$ of $b$ objects, the combined collection has $a + b$ objects. The sign $+$ is read "plus"; $a$ and $b$ are the addends (or terms), and $a + b$ is their sum. The count does not depend on which collections are used: if $A'$ and $B'$ are other disjoint collections of $a$ and $b$ objects, match $A$ one to one with $A'$ and $B$ with $B'$; together these match the two combined collections one to one, so they have the same number of objects.

To compute a sum, count on: start at the word for $a$ and say $b$ more number words; the word reached is $a + b$. This is proved by induction on $b$. For $b = 0$ nothing is added and the count stays $a$. If counting on $b$ words gives $a + b$, then one more object in the second collection is one more object in the whole, so the whole is counted by the next word: $a + (b + 1) = (a + b) + 1$, which is one more word of counting on. For $8 + 5$: nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, so $8 + 5 = 13$.

blocks.title: Difference
blocks.body:
Let $a$ and $b$ be whole numbers with $b \le a$. The difference $a - b$, read "$a$ minus $b$", is the whole number $c$ such that

$$b + c = a.$$

The number $a$ is called the minuend and $b$ the subtrahend. In words: $a - b$ is the missing addend, the number that must be added to $b$ to make $a$.

If $b > a$, then $b + c \ge b > a$ for every whole number $c$, so no whole number fits and $a - b$ is not defined among whole numbers. It becomes a number, a negative one, only when the number system is enlarged.

blocks.title: The difference exists and is unique
blocks.body: If $b \le a$, there is exactly one whole number $c$ with $b + c = a$.

Existence: take a collection of $a$ objects and set aside $b$ of them, which is possible since $b \le a$. Call the number of objects not set aside $c$. The two groups are disjoint and together make the original collection, so $b + c = a$.

Uniqueness: suppose $b + c = a$ and $b + c' = a$ with $c < c'$. Existence, applied to $c \le c'$, gives a $d$ with $c + d = c'$, and $d \ge 1$ since $d = 0$ would give $c' = c$. Then, by the associative law, $b + c' = b + (c + d) = (b + c) + d = a + d$, and $a + d > a$ because a collection of $a + d$ consists of $a$ objects and at least one more. This contradicts $b + c' = a$, so $c = c'$.

blocks.title: Three readings of subtraction give one number
blocks.body:
For $b \le a$, each of the following equals $a - b$:

1. Take away: the number of objects left when $b$ are removed from a collection of $a$.
2. Missing addend, or distance: the number of steps in counting on from $b$ to $a$; on the number line, the distance from the point $b$ to the point $a$.
3. Comparison: the number of objects of the larger collection left unmatched when a collection of $a$ and a collection of $b$ are paired off one to one.

The distance reading is the one that carries over to larger numbers: the distance can be measured in convenient jumps, and it does not change when both points slide the same way along the line (Compensation, below).

In each case the number $c$ described satisfies $b + c = a$, so by uniqueness it is $a - b$. In reading 1, the $b$ removed objects and the $c$ left are disjoint and make up the $a$. In reading 2, counting on $c$ steps from $b$ reaches $b + c$, as shown for the sum, and this is $a$; the steps are the unit lengths between $b$ and $a$. In reading 3, the matched objects of the larger collection are $b$ in number, one for each object of the smaller, and the matched and unmatched objects together are all $a$ of the larger collection.

blocks.title: Addition and subtraction undo each other
blocks.body:
For all whole numbers $a$ and $b$,

$$(a + b) - b = a, \qquad (a - b) + b = a \ \text{ if } b \le a.$$

Adding $b$ and then subtracting $b$, or the other way round, returns the starting number: the two operations are inverse operations. Combined with $a + b = b + a$, one fact $a + b = c$ yields four:

$$a + b = c, \; b + a = c, \; c - b = a, \; c - a = b.$$

So $a + b = c$ and $c - b = a$ are not two facts but one relation between three numbers, read with a different number as the unknown.

By definition, $(a + b) - b$ is the unique $c$ with $b + c = a + b$. The number $a$ qualifies, because $b + a = a + b$ (the commutative law, [[properties-of-operations]]); so $(a + b) - b = a$. For the second, $c = a - b$ means $b + c = a$, hence $c + b = b + c = a$. The fact family follows by applying the definition to $a + b = c$ and to $b + a = c$.
Compute $13 - 8$ by taking away and by counting on, and check the answer.
blocks.solution:
Taking away 8 from 13 means 8 steps back from 13, ending at 5. Counting on from 8 to 13 takes only 5 steps (2 to reach 10, then 3), so again $13 - 8 = 5$, as the theorem promises. When the subtrahend is close to the minuend, counting up from it, that is, measuring the distance, is the shorter route.

Check by the inverse: $8 + 5 = 13$.

blocks.body: Find the unknown number in each equation: (a) $\square + 6 = 15$; (b) $15 - \square = 6$; (c) $\square - 6 = 9$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $\square + 6 = 15$ says $6 + \square = 15$, so $\square = 15 - 6 = 9$.

(b) $15 - \square = 6$ says that $\square + 6 = 15$, the same equation as (a), so $\square = 9$.

(c) $\square - 6 = 9$ says $6 + 9 = \square$, so $\square = 15$. Here the unknown is the minuend, the whole, and it is found by adding, even though the equation contains a minus sign.

In each case the unknown can be anywhere, and the definition of the difference turns the equation into a statement about one sum $6 + 9 = 15$. (The equal sign means that the two sides are the same number, not "the answer comes next"; see [[equality-equal-sign]].)

blocks.title: Subtraction cannot be reordered or regrouped
blocks.body:
Addition can be done in any order, but subtraction cannot: $5 - 3 = 2$, while $3 - 5$ is not a whole number at all (it is the negative number $-2$). A common slip is to subtract "the smaller from the larger" whichever way round a difference is written.

Grouping matters too: $(9 - 4) - 2 = 3$ but $9 - (4 - 2) = 7$. Taking away 4 and then 2 is taking away $4 + 2$, so the correct rule is $(a - b) - c = a - (b + c)$.

items.q: What are $a - 0$ and $a - a$, and why?
items.a: $a - 0 = a$, because $0 + a = a$; and $a - a = 0$, because $a + 0 = a$.

items.q: A temperature rises from 13 °C to 21 °C. Which reading of subtraction gives the rise, and what is it?
items.a: Missing addend, or distance: nothing is taken away; the rise is what must be added to 13 to reach 21. From 13 it is 7 to 20 and 1 more to 21, so the rise is $21 - 13 = 8$ degrees, and $13 + 8 = 21$.

items.q: Compute $17 - 9$ by counting on, and check by adding.
items.solution: From 9: ten, eleven, ..., seventeen is 8 steps, so $17 - 9 = 8$. Check: $9 + 8 = 17$.

items.q: Show that $a - b \le a$ for $b \le a$, with equality only when $b = 0$.
items.solution: By definition $a = b + (a - b) \ge a - b$, since $b \ge 0$. If $a - b = a$, then $b + a = a = 0 + a$, so $b$ and $0$ are both the difference $a - a$, and by uniqueness $b = 0$.

items.q: For which whole numbers $a$ and $b$ are both $a - b$ and $b - a$ defined, and when are they equal?
items.hint: Each needs the subtrahend to be at most the minuend.
items.solution: $a - b$ needs $b \le a$ and $b - a$ needs $a \le b$, so both are defined only when $a = b$. Then both are 0, so they are equal exactly in that case.

items.q: Prove that $(a - b) - c = a - (b + c)$ whenever $b + c \le a$.
items.hint: Let $d = (a - b) - c$ and show that $(b + c) + d = a$.
items.solution: First, $b + c \le a$ gives $c \le a - b$ (since $b + c \le b + (a - b)$), so $d = (a - b) - c$ is defined, and by definition $c + d = a - b$. Hence $b + (c + d) = a$, which by the associative law is $(b + c) + d = a$. By the definition of the difference, $d = a - (b + c)$.

blocks.title: Situations and unknowns
blocks.body: Every addition or subtraction situation links three numbers by a single equation $\text{whole} = \text{part} + \text{part}$, and any one of the three may be unknown. An unknown whole is the sum of the parts; an unknown part is the whole minus the known part, by the definition of the difference. So the real question in a word problem is which number is the whole. The four standard families differ in the story, not in this mathematics.

blocks.title: The four situation families
blocks.body:
1. Add to: $\text{start} + \text{change} = \text{result}$; the result is the whole.
2. Take from: $\text{start} - \text{change} = \text{result}$; the start is the whole.
3. Put together or take apart: $\text{part} + \text{part} = \text{total}$, with nothing changing; the total is the whole.
4. Compare: $\text{smaller} + \text{difference} = \text{bigger}$; the bigger amount is the whole.

A bar model, or tape diagram, draws the equation: the bar for the whole is exactly as long as the bars of the parts laid end to end.

blocks.caption: Bar model for: route B is 5 km shorter than route A, and route B is 8 km. Route A's bar is route B's 8 and 5 more, so route A is $8 + 5 = 13$ km, though the word shorter suggests subtracting.
blocks.alt: Two horizontal bars starting at the same place. The lower bar, labelled route B, is 8 long. The upper bar, labelled route A, is made of a white piece 8 long and a hatched blue piece 5 long. A double arrow over the upper bar is labelled ? = 13.

blocks.title: Key words can point the wrong way
blocks.body:
"Fewer", "less" and "shorter" do not always mean subtract, nor "more" add. In the figure's problem the answer is $8 + 5$. Compare problems worded like this, together with add-to and take-from problems whose start is unknown, are the situations learners find hardest.

Some phrases also reverse the written order: "5 less than 8" is $8 - 5$, and "subtract 24 from 43" is $43 - 24 = 19$. Decide the operation from which number is the whole, not from the words.
A bus carries 23 people. At the first stop 8 get off; at the second, 5 get on. How many are on the bus now?
blocks.solution:
Step by step: $23 - 8 = 15$, then $15 + 5 = 20$.

Or combine the changes first: 8 off and 5 on is a net change of $8 - 5 = 3$ off, and $23 - 3 = 20$. The two routes agree because $(a - b) + c = a - (b - c)$ when $c \le b \le a$: both sides plus $b - c$ give $a$.

items.q: In a survey, 37% of those asked answered yes and everyone else answered no. Write two different equations for the percentage answering no, and solve them.
items.hint: Put together with one part unknown; the whole is 100%.
items.solution: $37 + \square = 100$ and $100 - 37 = \square$. Both say that the yes and no percentages make the whole 100%, so $\square = 63$: 63% answered no. Either equation matches the situation; what matters is that 100 is the whole.

items.q: Write as an expression and evaluate: the difference of 13 and 8; 6 less than 20; 15 subtracted from 40.
items.hint: Two of the three phrases reverse the order in which the numbers are said.

items.q: A bank balance is 64. Payments of 18 and 27 go out and 40 comes in. (a) What is the balance afterwards? (b) With the same three transactions, what starting balance would end at 50?
items.hint: Find the net change first. In (b) the start is the unknown whole.
items.solution:
(a) Step by step: $64 - 18 = 46$, $46 - 27 = 19$, $19 + 40 = 59$. By net change: $18 + 27 = 45$ out and 40 in is a net 5 out, and $64 - 5 = 59$.

(b) Now the start is unknown: $\square - 5 = 50$, so $\square = 50 + 5 = 55$. Check: $55 - 18 = 37$, $37 - 27 = 10$, $10 + 40 = 50$.

items.q: A take-from situation reads $\text{start} - \text{change} = \text{result}$. Explain why it is solved by an addition when the start is unknown, $\square - b = r$, but by a subtraction when the change is unknown, $a - \square = r$, and give both answers.
items.hint: In each case, which number is the whole, and is it known?
items.solution: In both, the start is the whole, made of the change and the result. In $\square - b = r$ the definition of the difference gives $b + r = \square$: the whole is unknown, so it is the sum, $\square = r + b$. In $a - \square = r$ it gives $\square + r = a$: the whole $a$ is known and a part is missing, so $\square = a - r$ (which needs $r \le a$). The word take appears in both; only the position of the unknown decides the operation.

blocks.title: Facts within 20
blocks.body: By place value, every calculation with larger numbers comes down to sums of two one-digit numbers and the subtractions that undo them. These facts are the steps of every longer calculation, so having them at hand, from memory or in one quick step from a landmark such as ten or a double, is what makes larger calculations fast and reliable. They are few, and the table below holds them all.

blocks.title: The addition table
blocks.body:
There are 100 sums $a + b$ with $a$ and $b$ in $\{0, 1, \dots, 9\}$.

1. Every subtraction $c - b$ with $b$ and $c - b$ one-digit is one of these sums read backwards, so the table holds the subtraction facts too.
2. Since $a + b = b + a$, only 55 of the sums are different facts.
3. Exactly 45 of the 100 are 10 or more. These are the pairs of ones digits that force a regroup when two numbers are added by place value, and the sums for which making ten is the useful route.

1. If $c - b = a$ then $c = b + a$, which is in the table.

2. Count unordered pairs: 10 doubles $a + a$, and $\frac{10 \times 9}{2} = 45$ pairs with $a < b$, giving $10 + 45 = 55$.

3. For a fixed $a$, the sum is at least 10 exactly when $b \ge 10 - a$; with $b \le 9$ that leaves the $a$ values $b = 10 - a, \dots, 9$. Adding over $a = 0, 1, \dots, 9$ gives $0 + 1 + \dots + 9 = 45$.

blocks.caption: The addition table: row $a$, column $b$ holds $a + b$. The 45 shaded entries are 10 or more. The circled diagonal holds the doubles, and the table is symmetric about it because $a + b = b + a$. Each sum $s$ fills one line running from lower left to upper right, and that line has $10 - |s - 9|$ entries (last exercise below). To read $c - b$, go along row $b$ to the entry $c$: its column is $c - b$.
blocks.alt: A 10 by 10 grid with rows and columns labelled 0 to 9. Each cell shows the row number plus the column number. Cells whose value is 10 or more are shaded orange in a staircase in the lower right half. The diagonal cells 0, 2, 4, up to 18 are circled in blue.

blocks.title: Three routes to 8 + 7
blocks.body: None of these needs counting; each turns the sum into an easier one using a known landmark.

items.label: Make ten
items.body: Split 7 as $2 + 5$ to complete the 8 to ten: $8 + 7 = 8 + 2 + 5 = 10 + 5 = 15$.

blocks.body: Find $15 - 7$ by thinking of the addition, and by going down through ten.
blocks.solution:
Addition: $7 + \square = 15$. From 7, it is 3 to reach 10 and then 5 more to 15, so $\square = 3 + 5 = 8$. This is right because $7 + (3 + 5) = (7 + 3) + 5 = 10 + 5 = 15$, so $3 + 5$ is the missing addend.

Down through ten: take the 7 away in two pieces, first 5 to reach 10, then 2: $15 - 5 - 2 = 10 - 2 = 8$. This is the rule $(a - b) - c = a - (b + c)$ of the first section, proved in its exercises, with $a = 15$, $b = 5$, $c = 2$.

Order and grouping of a sum may be changed freely ([[properties-of-operations]]), so pair the 4 with the 6: $4 + 7 + 6 = (4 + 6) + 7 = 10 + 7 = 17$. Looking for a pair that makes ten is quickest to add three or more one-digit numbers.

items.q: Where in the addition table is the answer to $14 - 9$?
items.a: In row 9 (or column 9), at the entry 14: it is in column 5 (or row 5), since $9 + 5 = 14$. So $14 - 9 = 5$.

items.q: Find $6 + 8$ in two different ways.
items.hint: Make ten, or use a double.
items.solution: Make ten: $8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 14$. Double: $6 + 8 = 6 + 6 + 2 = 12 + 2 = 14$, or $7 + 7 = 14$ after moving 1 from the 8 to the 6.

items.q: Find $16 - 9$ by thinking of an addition.
items.solution: From 9 it is 1 to 10 and then 6 to 16, so $16 - 9 = 1 + 6 = 7$. Check: $9 + 7 = 16$.

items.hint: Look for pairs that make ten.

items.q: Prove that making ten always works: if $a$ and $b$ are digits with $a + b \ge 10$, then $a + b = 10 + e$, where $e = b - (10 - a)$ is a digit from 0 to 8.
items.hint: Why is $10 - a \le b$? Then split $b$ as $(10 - a) + e$.
items.solution: If $b < 10 - a$, then $a + b < a + (10 - a) = 10$; so $a + b \ge 10$ forces $b \ge 10 - a$, and $e = b - (10 - a)$ is defined, with $b = (10 - a) + e$. Regrouping, $a + b = \big(a + (10 - a)\big) + e = 10 + e$. Finally $e \le 8$ because $10 + e = a + b \le 9 + 9 = 18$. For $8 + 7$: $10 - 8 = 2$ and $e = 7 - 2 = 5$, so $8 + 7 = 15$.

items.q: Show that each sum $s$ from 0 to 18 appears $10 - |s - 9|$ times in the table, and check that these counts add up to 100.
items.hint: Count the $a$ in $0, \dots, 9$ for which $b = s - a$ is also in $0, \dots, 9$.
items.solution: We need $0 \le a \le 9$ and $0 \le s - a \le 9$, that is $\max(0, s - 9) \le a \le \min(9, s)$. For $s \le 9$ this is $0 \le a \le s$: $s + 1 = 10 - (9 - s)$ values. For $s \ge 9$ it is $s - 9 \le a \le 9$: $19 - s = 10 - (s - 9)$ values. Either way the count is $10 - |s - 9|$. Total: $(1 + 2 + \dots + 10) + (9 + 8 + \dots + 1) = 55 + 45 = 100$; the sums $s \ge 10$ alone give $9 + 8 + \dots + 1 = 45$, the shaded entries.

blocks.title: Larger numbers by place value
blocks.body:
A two- or three-digit number is a sum of hundreds, tens and ones ([[place-value]]). Since a sum can be reordered and regrouped freely ([[properties-of-operations]]), two such numbers are added unit by unit: hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens, ones with ones. Tens behave like ones, because 3 tens and 4 tens are 7 tens, so $30 + 40 = 70$ is the fact $3 + 4 = 7$ about tens.

There is one complication each way. In addition, a unit may total ten or more, and ten of it are regrouped as one of the next unit. In subtraction, a unit may have too few, and one of the next unit is regrouped as ten. The written column methods ([[column-addition-subtraction]]) set out exactly these steps in a fixed layout; here they are written in a line, as in mental calculation.

blocks.title: Adding and subtracting unit by unit
blocks.body:
For any whole numbers $a, b, c, d$, not only digits,

$$(10a + b) + (10c + d) = 10(a + c) + (b + d),$$

and, if $c \le a$ and $d \le b$,

$$(10a + b) - (10c + d) = 10(a - c) + (b - d).$$

For two-digit numbers, where $a, b, c, d$ are digits:

1. If $b + d \ge 10$, write $b + d = 10 + e$; the sum is $10(a + c + 1) + e$, one ten more.
2. If $10c + d \le 10a + b$ and $d \le b$, then $c \le a$ follows, and the subtraction is done unit by unit.
3. If $10c + d \le 10a + b$ but $d > b$, then $c \le a - 1$. Rewrite $10a + b = 10(a - 1) + (10 + b)$, one ten as ten ones; now $c \le a - 1$ and $d \le 10 + b$, so the rule applies with tens $a - 1$ and ones $10 + b$.

Three-digit numbers $100p + 10q + r$ work the same way, with hundreds as a third unit: sums and differences go unit by unit, and $(100p + 10q + r) - (100s + 10t + u) = 100(p - s) + 10(q - t) + (r - u)$ whenever $s \le p$, $t \le q$, $u \le r$. When a unit of the top number is short, regroup one of the next unit up as ten, starting from the ones. If that next digit is 0, as the tens of 503 are, a hundred must first become ten tens: $503 = 400 + 100 + 3 = 400 + 90 + 13$.

Addition: reorder and regroup, $(10a + b) + (10c + d) = (10a + 10c) + (b + d)$, and $a$ tens and $c$ tens are $a + c$ tens. If $b + d = 10 + e$, the extra 10 is one more ten.

Subtraction: by the definition of the difference it is enough to check that the proposed answer plus $10c + d$ gives $10a + b$. Indeed $10(a - c) + (b - d) + 10c + d = 10a + b$, adding tens to tens and ones to ones. Nothing here needs digits.

For digits: if $c \ge a + 1$, then $10c + d \ge 10a + 10 > 10a + b$, because $b \le 9$; so $10c + d \le 10a + b$ forces $c \le a$. If also $d > b$, then $10c + d \le 10a + b < 10a + d$ gives $10c < 10a$, so $c \le a - 1$. The rewriting in case 3 changes the units but not the number, since $10(a - 1) + 10 = 10a$; its tens $a - 1$ and ones $10 + b$ need not be digits, which is why the rule was stated for all whole numbers.

Three digits: the check is the same with three units, and each regrouping keeps the number. A unit is regrouped only when it is short, so afterwards each unit of the top number exceeds the matching unit below by at most 9. Then if the hundreds left, $p'$, were fewer than $s$, the top number would be at most $100(s - 1) + 99 + (10t + u) < 100s + 10t + u$, contradicting that it is the larger. So the hundreds always suffice.

blocks.caption: $43 - 26$ with base-ten blocks. 43 is 4 tens and 3 ones. Since 6 ones cannot be taken from 3, one ten becomes a row of 10 ones (hatched), giving 3 tens and 13 ones, still 43. Taking away 2 tens and 6 ones (crossed out) leaves 1 ten and 7 ones (boxed): $43 - 26 = 17$.
blocks.alt: Left: four rods of ten squares and three single squares, labelled 43: 4 tens, 3 ones. An arrow points right to three rods, a row of ten hatched blue squares and three white squares above its left end, labelled 3 tens, 13 ones. Two rods and the last six hatched squares are crossed out in red. A dashed green box holds the remaining rod and seven squares, labelled left: 1 ten, 7 ones = 17.

blocks.body: Compute $456 + 376$. Estimate first, and check the answer with the inverse.
blocks.solution:
Estimate: $456 + 376$ is close to $460 + 380 = 840$.

Unit by unit: hundreds $400 + 300 = 700$, tens $50 + 70 = 120$, ones $6 + 6 = 12$. So

$$\begin{aligned} 456 + 376 &= 700 + 120 + 12 \\ &= 700 + 130 + 2 = 832. \end{aligned}$$

The ones regrouped once (12 ones are 1 ten and 2 ones) and the tens once (13 tens are 1 hundred and 3 tens). The answer is near the estimate. Check: $832 - 376 = 456$.

blocks.body: Compute $503 - 278$.
blocks.solution:
The ones digit 3 is less than 8, and there are no tens to regroup, so regroup a hundred first: $503 = 400 + 100 + 3 = 400 + 90 + 13$. Now subtract unit by unit:

$$\begin{aligned} 503 - 278 &= (400 - 200) + (90 - 70) + (13 - 8) \\ &= 200 + 20 + 5 = 225. \end{aligned}$$

Check: $225 + 278 = 503$. Estimate: $500 - 280 = 220$, close.

blocks.title: Compensation
blocks.body:
For whole numbers $a, b, k$,

$$(a + k) + (b - k) = a + b \ \ (k \le b), \qquad (a + k) - (b + k) = a - b \ \ (b \le a).$$

A sum does not change if one addend gives some to the other: $28 + 16 = 30 + 14 = 44$. A difference does not change if both numbers are increased, or both decreased, by the same amount: $74 - 38 = 76 - 40 = 36$.

First: $(a + k) + (b - k) = a + \big(k + (b - k)\big) = a + b$, by regrouping and the definition of $b - k$.

Second: $(b + k) + (a - b) = \big(b + (a - b)\big) + k = a + k$, so by the definition of the difference $(a + k) - (b + k) = a - b$. In the distance reading of the first section, a difference is the distance between two points on the number line, and moving both points the same way by the same amount keeps their distance ([[number-line]]).

blocks.title: Three ways to compute 62 - 28
blocks.body: Each method is one of the facts above; which is quickest depends on the numbers.

items.label: Count up
items.body: Read it as $28 + \square = 62$ and jump along the number line to landmarks: $28 \to 30 \to 60 \to 62$, jumps of $2 + 30 + 2 = 34$.

items.label: Same difference
items.body: Add 2 to both numbers to make the subtrahend a multiple of ten: $62 - 28 = 64 - 30 = 34$.

blocks.caption: Top: $62 - 28$ by counting up from 28, with jumps of 2, 30 and 2 to the landmarks 30, 60 and 62. Bottom: the segments from 28 to 62 and from 30 to 64 have the same length 34, so $62 - 28 = 64 - 30$.
blocks.alt: Two number lines. The upper one is marked 28, 30, 60, 62, with curved arrows from 28 to 30 labelled +2, from 30 to 60 labelled +30 and from 60 to 62 labelled +2. The lower one is marked 28, 30, 62, 64, with a green segment from 28 to 62 labelled 62 - 28 and a dashed purple segment from 30 to 64 labelled 64 - 30, of equal length.

items.a: The first is true: both numbers were decreased by 4, and both sides are 36. The second is false: 74 went up by 2 but 38 went down by 2, so $76 - 36 = 40$ is 4 more than $74 - 38 = 36$.

items.q: Compute mentally $640 - 10$, $607 - 100$ and $395 + 10$.
items.hint: Adding or subtracting a ten or a hundred changes one digit, unless that digit passes 9 or 0.
items.solution: $640 - 10 = 630$; $607 - 100 = 507$; $395 + 10 = 405$, where the 9 tens become 10 tens, which regroup as a hundred.

items.q: Compute $700 - 268$ in two ways.
items.hint: Regroup $700$ as $600 + 90 + 10$, or subtract 1 from both numbers.
items.solution: Regrouping: $(600 - 200) + (90 - 60) + (10 - 8) = 400 + 30 + 2 = 432$. Same difference: $700 - 268 = 699 - 267 = 432$, with no regrouping at all since every digit of 699 is at least the digit below it. Check: $432 + 268 = 700$.

items.q: Someone computes $52 - 27 = 35$. Find the error, and show how the inverse check exposes it.
items.hint: Look at what happened to the ones.
items.solution: They took 2 from 7 in the ones instead of 7 from 2, getting $30 + 5 = 35$. Correct: $52 = 40 + 12$, so $(40 - 20) + (12 - 7) = 20 + 5 = 25$. The check catches it: $35 + 27 = 62 \ne 52$, while $25 + 27 = 52$.

items.q: A common slip is to compensate in opposite directions, writing $74 - 38 = 76 - 36$. Show that $(a + k) - (b - k) = (a - b) + 2k$ when $k \le b \le a$, so the slip is always off by exactly $2k$, and explain why the inverse check catches it whenever $k \ge 1$.
items.hint: Add $b - k$ to the proposed right side.
items.solution: $(b - k) + \big((a - b) + 2k\big) = \big((b - k) + k\big) + (a - b) + k = b + (a - b) + k = a + k$, so by the definition of the difference $(a + k) - (b - k) = (a - b) + 2k$. For $74 - 38$ with $k = 2$: $76 - 36 = 40 = 36 + 4$. The inverse check adds the original subtrahend to the claimed answer and gets $(a - b) + 2k + b = a + 2k$, which is not $a$ when $k \ge 1$; here $40 + 38 = 78 \ne 74$.

items.q: When $n$ numbers are added unit by unit ($n \ge 2$), show that the carry into each unit is at most $n - 1$. What is the bound for two numbers, and for three?
items.hint: Induction from the ones: bound the total in a unit when the carry into it is at most $n - 1$.
items.solution: Nothing is carried into the ones. If the carry into a unit is at most $n - 1$, the total there is at most $9n + (n - 1) = 10n - 1 < 10n$, so it makes at most $n - 1$ of the next unit. By induction every carry is at most $n - 1$: at most 1 for two numbers ($9 + 9 + 1 = 19$) and at most 2 for three ($9 + 9 + 9 + 2 = 29$), as in $999 + 999 + 999 = 2997$.

rows.text: Changing ten ones into a ten, or a ten into ten ones, is called carrying and borrowing in many American books, exchanging in England, and composing or decomposing a ten in some newer materials. This page calls both directions regrouping.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
The unit-by-unit steps become the written [[column-addition-subtraction|column methods]], which work for numbers of any length. Reading an equation such as $\square - 6 = 9$ as a statement about one sum is the start of solving equations ([[equality-equal-sign]]), and the laws used throughout, that a sum can be reordered and regrouped, are the subject of [[properties-of-operations]]. Adding the same number repeatedly is [[multiplication]].

Subtraction $a - b$ fails among whole numbers when $b > a$. Enlarging the number system so that every subtraction is possible gives the integers, in which $a - b = a + (-b)$: subtracting is adding an inverse. A set with an associative operation, an identity and an inverse for every element is a [[groups|group]], and clock arithmetic, where $9 + 5 = 2$ on a 12-hour clock, is another example ([[congruences]]).

Addition need not be taken on trust from collections of objects. It can be defined from counting alone, by $a + 0 = a$ and $a + (b + 1) = (a + b) + 1$, which is counting on written as a rule; the commutative and associative laws can then be proved by [[induction]].

- $a + b$ counts a collection of $a$ together with a disjoint collection of $b$; for $b \le a$, $a - b$ is the unique $c$ with $b + c = a$.
- Take away, missing addend (the distance from $b$ to $a$ on the number line) and comparison are three readings of the same number $a - b$.
- Adding and subtracting the same number undo each other: $a + b = c$ and $c - b = a$ are one relation. Subtraction cannot be reordered or regrouped.
- In a word problem, find the whole: an unknown whole is a sum, an unknown part a difference, whatever the key words.
- Facts within 20 follow from ten and doubles; larger numbers are added and subtracted unit by unit with regrouping, and compensation keeps a sum or a difference unchanged.
